etymologies.etymologyHTML: From French district, from Medieval Latin districtus (“a district within which the lord may distrain, also jurisdiction”), from Latin districtus, past participle of distringere (“to draw asunder, compel, distrain”), from dis- (“apart”) +‎ stringere (“to draw tight, strain”). Doublet of Detroit.

definitions.definition: An administrative division of an area.

quote.citation: 1963, Margery Allingham, “Foreword”, in The China Governess: A Mystery, London: Chatto & Windus, →OCLC:
quote.text: ‘I understand that the district was considered a sort of sanctuary,’ the Chief was saying. ‘An Alsatia like the ancient one behind the Strand, or the Saffron Hill before the First World War. […]’

definitions.definition: An area or region marked by some distinguishing feature.
(UK) An administrative division of a county without the status of a borough.
(mining) A specific, usually named area of the coalface where particular seams are worked.
(transitive) To divide into administrative or other districts.

quote.citation: 1563 March 30 (Gregorian calendar), John Foxe, Actes and Monuments of These Latter and Perillous Dayes, […], London:  […]  Iohn Day, […], →OCLC:
quote.text: punishing with the rod of district severity
